name: Sower Sunday
description: The parable of the sower and the reception of God's word.
biblicalBasis: Jesus tells the parable of the sower who scatters seed in different types of soil (Matt 13:1-23, Mark 4:1-20, Luke 8:4-15). Some falls on the path and birds eat it, some on rocky ground where it withers quickly, some among thorns that choke it, and some in good soil where it bears fruit—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, a hundredfold. Jesus explains that the seed is God's word and the soil represents human hearts.
significance: The parable addresses how people receive God's word—and what hinders it from bearing fruit: indifference, shallow faith, worries, and wealth. At the same time, it is a promise: where the word takes root, it bears abundant fruit. The responsibility lies with the receiver, but the power resides in the word itself.
liturgicalContext: Green color (Ordinary Time). Placed between Epiphany and Lent. The focus on God's word makes this day a natural transition—from revelation to discipleship.
history: Sower Sunday is particularly important in Scandinavian Lutheran tradition. Luther placed great emphasis on the parable as a description of the effect of the word and the challenges of faith. This day has traditionally been linked to Bible distribution and mission work.
otConnections: Isaiah 55:10-11—God's word like rain that does not return without accomplishing what it was sent for. Psalm 126:5-6 about sowing in tears and reaping with joy. Isaiah 6:9-10 about the people who hear but do not understand—quoted by Jesus in his explanation of the parable.

references.reason: The day is directly named after and defined by the parable of the sower (Matt 13:1-23). The text contains the parable itself and Jesus' explanation of how God's word is received in different hearts.

The parable of the weeds in the field is a central part of the chapter often preached together with the parable of the sower on this day to illustrate the growth of God's kingdom and the final judgment.
The parables of the mustard seed and yeast are part of the same teaching session in Matt 13 proclaimed on Sower Sunday, illustrating the growth of the kingdom of heaven.
The transitional verses summarizing Jesus' use of parables and linking it to prophecy (Isa 6:9-10) are an integral part of the theological message of the chapter on Sower Sunday.
Jesus' explanation of the parable of the weeds (continued from verse 24), which expands on the theme of judgment and the nature of God's kingdom, is a natural part of the reading for Sower Sunday.

The parables of the treasure in the field, the pearl of great value, and the net are part of the same chapter (Matt 13) and deal with the value of the kingdom of heaven and the final separation, often read together on this day.
The conclusion of the chapter with Jesus' rejection in his hometown shows the consequence of not understanding the parables and serves as a natural ending to the reading for the day.
